summaries.title: Distributed Representations: Composition & Superposition
summaries.gist: Distributed representations combine two distinct, mutually competing strategies—composition and superposition—that must be told apart to understand neural network representations.
summaries.question: Distributed representations — how do composition and superposition relate? (an argued distinction)

summaries.title: Intro & Codes
summaries.gist: Distributed representations split into composition and superposition, two properties with different generalization and computation profiles, illustrated via Thorpe's shape-color neuron codes.
summaries.question: Distributed representations — what are the basic code types that reveal composition versus superposition? (four example codes)

summaries.title: Framing the note
summaries.gist: This note revisits distributed representations to separate composition and superposition, arguing they trade off and matter for escaping the curse of dimensionality.

summaries.title: Thorpe's examples and binary focus
summaries.gist: Thorpe's four shape-color codes, reinterpreted along composition and superposition axes rather than a local-distributed spectrum, are restricted here to binary neuron activations for tractability.

summaries.title: "Local" Codes
summaries.gist: A local code assigning one neuron per shape-color pair is monosemantic and superposition-free, yet still supports flexible linear selection of arbitrary stimulus sets.
summaries.question: "Local" Codes — what can a monosemantic local code actually do? (worked example)

summaries.title: Local code properties
summaries.gist: Despite seeming wasteful, the local code lets a later layer linearly select arbitrary combinations of stimuli, such as black circles and white triangles but not their opposites.

summaries.title: Linear probes caveat
summaries.gist: A linear probe could successfully detect "red" in this local code, yet the representation still should not be described as containing a genuine red feature.

summaries.title: "Semi-Local" / Compositional Codes
summaries.gist: Compositional codes represent independent features like color and shape that combine, giving fewer neurons, statistical efficiency, extensibility, and clean interpretability.
summaries.question: "Semi-Local" / Compositional Codes — what makes composition advantageous? (three advantages)

summaries.title: Compositional feature structure
summaries.gist: Representing colors and shapes as separate composing features, as in Mikolov's word embeddings, defines what is usually meant by distributed representations in machine learning.

summaries.title: Advantages of composition
summaries.gist: Composition needs exponentially fewer neurons than pairs, enables non-local generalization across shared features, and extends naturally to intermediate or uncertain objects.

summaries.title: Interpretability benefit
summaries.gist: Compositional representations remain interpretable because they can be understood component by component, even though the space of combinations grows exponentially.

summaries.title: "Dense" / Maximal Superposition Codes
summaries.gist: Maximal superposition packs exponentially many stimuli into few neurons but sacrifices linear probeability and the ability to represent intermediate objects, requiring non-composing features.
summaries.question: "Dense" / Maximal Superposition Codes — what does maximal superposition cost in exchange for its capacity? (worked example)

summaries.title: Capacity and its costs
summaries.gist: A dense four-neuron code can represent sixteen colored shapes, but loses the ability to linearly probe individual features or represent intermediate combinations.

summaries.title: Why composition is dropped
summaries.gist: Achieving maximal superposition requires reverting to combined color-shape features rather than independent composing ones, since superposition and composition cannot coexist fully.

summaries.title: Composition vs Superposition
summaries.gist: Composition and superposition are not points on one distributed-ness spectrum but orthogonal strategies competing for the same exponential volume of representational space.
summaries.question: Composition vs Superposition — why are these two strategies fundamentally in tension? (a volume argument)

summaries.title: Beyond a single spectrum
summaries.gist: The apparent trend from local to semi-local to highly-distributed codes actually hides two orthogonal strategies, composition and superposition, rather than one continuum.

summaries.title: The volume trade-off
summaries.gist: With m bits giving exp(m) volume, fully composable features consume volume as exp(n), so full composition and full superposition cannot both be maximized at once.

summaries.title: Why the distinction matters
summaries.gist: Because composition and superposition trade off, treating them as one property wrongly implies non-local generalization and neuron-exceeding capacity come together for free.

summaries.title: Mixing Composition and Superposition
summaries.gist: When features are sparse rather than dense, composition leaves unused regions of representational space that can be filled with superposed features, as Thorpe's semi-distributed code shows.
summaries.question: Mixing Composition and Superposition — how can composition and superposition coexist despite competing? (a worked example)

summaries.title: Sparsity enables mixing
summaries.gist: Sparse, mutually exclusive feature combinations create low-probability holes in compositional space, and these holes can be exploited to store additional features in superposition.

summaries.title: Semi-distributed code revisited
summaries.gist: Thorpe's semi-distributed code composes color and shape features while placing colors in mutual superposition and shapes in mutual superposition, best read as directions, not single neurons.

summaries.title: Conclusion
summaries.gist: Distinguishing composition from superposition matters because their differing properties determine whether representations can be understood with linear rather than exponential effort.
summaries.question: Distributed representations — why does distinguishing composition from superposition matter for interpretability? (a closing claim)

summaries.title: Two tensions, one distinction
summaries.gist: Superposition and composition are the two things people conflate under "distributed representations," and though mixable, they remain fundamentally in tension with differing properties.

summaries.title: Stakes for interpretability
summaries.gist: Composition allows neural representations to be understood via a linear number of independent features instead of exponential volume, which is essential for truly understanding networks.

glossary.name: Superposition
glossary.senseHere: The strategy of encoding more features than there are neurons by using non-composing feature combinations as directions, so that exponentially many distinct items can be stored in a fixed number of neurons but only recovered with a non-linearity, not a linear probe.

glossary.name: Composition
glossary.senseHere: The strategy of representing independent features (like color and shape) separately so they can combine linearly into an exponential space of objects, allowing non-local generalization and linear selectability, but requiring exponential volume to do so fully.

glossary.name: Thorpe (1989)
glossary.background: A neuroscience paper by Simon Thorpe that introduced a spectrum of coding schemes—local, semi-local, semi-distributed, and highly-distributed—to illustrate different ways neurons might jointly represent stimuli.

glossary.name: Monosemantic
glossary.senseHere: Describes a neuron or unit that corresponds to a single, clean feature (such as one specific shape-color pair) rather than responding to multiple unrelated features.

glossary.name: Linear probe
glossary.senseHere: A method of testing whether a feature is represented by checking if a linear function of neuron activations can predict it; the piece cautions that a feature being linearly probeable doesn't necessarily mean the network truly has that feature as a component.

glossary.name: Toy Models of Superposition
glossary.senseHere: An earlier paper by the same research group that the note treats as having already explored the composition/superposition trade-off, though framed there in terms of feature sparsity rather than composition.
